notes.title: Sets
notes.html:
A set may be thought of as a collection of objects.

A set is usually described by listing or describing its members inside curly brackets. For example, when we write A={1,2,3}A = \{1, 2, 3\}, we mean that the objects belonging to the set AA are the numbers 1, 2, 3 (or, equivalently, the set AA consists of the numbers 1, 2 and 3).

When xx is an object in a set AA, we write x∈Ax \in A and say ‘xx belongs to AA’ or ‘xx is a member of AA’.

The set which has no members is called the empty set and is denoted by ∅\emptyset. The empty set may seem like a strange concept, but it has its uses.

We say that the set SS is a subset of the set TT, and we write S⊆TS \subseteq T, if every member of SS is a member of TT. For example, {1,2,3}⊆{1,2,3,5,6,40}\{1, 2, 3\} \subseteq \{1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 40\}. (Be aware that some texts use ⊂\subset where we use ⊆\subseteq.)
